semin-durr:1-1.t:
His saying: {والطارق}: al-ṭāriq is originally the active participle of ṭaraqa yaṭruqu ṭurūqan, i.e. he came by night. [The poet] said:
4539 - فمِثْلَكِ حُبْلى قد طَرَقْتُ ومُرْضِعاً ... فألهَيْتُها عن ذي تمائمَ مُحْوِلِ
(Many a woman like you, pregnant or nursing, have I visited by night, and distracted her from her year-old infant wearing amulets.)
Its origin is from striking. Al-ṭāriq bi-l-ḥaṣā is the one who strikes with pebbles [for divination]. [The poet] said:
4540 - لعَمْرُكَ ما تَدْري الضواربُ بالحصى ... ولا زاجراتُ الطيرِ ما اللَّهُ صانعُ
(By your life, neither the women who strike pebbles nor those who drive off birds [for omens] know what Allah will do.)
Then its use was extended, and everyone who comes by night was called ṭāriq.

semin-durr:4-4.t:
His saying: {إِن كُلُّ نَفْسٍ لَّمَّا عَلَيْهَا}: the light and the doubled forms of «لَمَّاً» were discussed in Sūrat Hūd. For whoever reads it light here, «إنْ» here is lightened from the heavy [inna] (mukhaffafa), «كلُّ» is a mubtadaʾ (subject), the lām is the distinguishing lām (al-lām al-fāriqa), «عليها» is a fronted khabar (predicate) and «حافظٌ» is a postponed mubtadaʾ, and the clause is the khabar of «كل», with «ما» redundant (zāʾida) after the distinguishing lām. Alternatively «عليها» alone may be the khabar, with «حافِظٌ» as its agent (fāʿil), which is better. Alternatively «كلُّ» may be a mubtadaʾ and «حافظٌ» its khabar, with «عليها» attached to it and «ما» also redundant. All of this branches from the view of the Basrans. The Kufans said: «إنْ» here is negative, the lām means «إلاَّ» (except), affirming after the negation, and «ما» is redundant. The discussion of this was given in full before.
As for the reading with doubling, «إنْ» is negative and «لَمَّا» means «إلاَّ»; the evidence for that was given in full in Hūd. Hārūn reported that «إنَّ» was read here with doubling and «كلَّ» in the accusative as its noun, the lām being the one that enters the predicate, «ما» redundant and «حافظٌ» its khabar. On every analysis, «إنْ» and what falls in its domain is the reply to the oath, whether one makes it the lightened form or the negative. It has also been said: the reply is {إِنَّهُ على رَجْعِهِ}, and what lies between is parenthetical (iʿtirāḍ); but this is far-fetched.

semin-durr:6-6.t: His saying: {دَافِقٍ}: it has been said: it is fāʿil (active) in the sense of mafʿūl (passive), the reverse of their saying «سيلٌ مُفْعَم» (a filled torrent) and of the saying of the Exalted {حِجَاباً مَّسْتُوراً} [al-Isrāʾ: 45] on one view. It has also been said: «دافق» is by way of relation (nasab), i.e. possessing gushing (dafq) or outpouring (indifāq). Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "It is valid for the water to be gushing (dāfiq), because part of it pushes (yadfuqu) another part, i.e. drives it; so some of it is gushing and some of it gushed." End of quote. Al-dafq is pouring, so its verb is transitive. Zayd ibn ʿAlī read «مَدْفُوقٍ» (poured), as though he was explaining the meaning.

semin-durr:7-7.t:
His saying: {والترآئب}: plural of tarība, which is the place of the necklace among the bones of the chest; because the child is created from the fluid of both of them: the man's fluid is in his loins (ṣulb) and the woman's in her breast-bones (tarāʾib). This is the meaning of his saying {مِن نُّطْفَةٍ أَمْشَاجٍ} [al-Insān: 2]. The poet said:
4540 - مُهَفْهَفَةٌ بيضاءُ غيرُ مُفاضَةٍ ... تَرائِبُها مَصْقُولةٌ كالسَّجَنْجَلِ
(Slender-waisted, fair, not paunchy, her breast-bones polished like a mirror.)
[Translator's note: the verse number 4540 is as printed; it repeats the number of an earlier verse.]
And he said:
4541 - والزَّعْفَرانُ على ترائبِها ... شَرِقَتْ به اللَّبَّاتُ والنَّحْرُ
(And saffron on her breast-bones, with which the upper chest and the throat are steeped.)
Abū ʿUbayda said: "The plural of tarība is tarīb." [The poet] said:
4542 - ومِنْ ذَهَبٍ يَذُوْبُ على تَرِيْبٍ ... كلَوْنِ العاجِ ليس بذي غُضونِ
(And of gold melting upon a breast the colour of ivory, without wrinkles.)
It has also been said: al-tarāʾib are the collarbones. It has also been said: the ribs of the man which are below the loins. It has also been said: what lies between the shoulders and the chest. From Ibn ʿAbbās: they are a person's extremities: his hands, his feet and his eyes. It has also been said: the essence of the heart. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "In these views there is arbitrariness regarding the language."
The majority read «يَخْرُج» in the active voice, and Ibn Abī ʿAbla and Ibn Miqsam in the passive. He also, and the people of Mecca, read «الصُّلُب» with ḍamma on the ṣād and the lām, and al-Yamānī with fatḥa on both; on this is the saying of al-ʿAjjāj:
4543 - في صَلَبٍ مِثْلِ العِنانِ المُؤْدَمِ
(In a back [ṣalab] like a rein of tanned leather.)
Its dialectal forms were given in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ. The strangest of them is «صالِب», as in [the poet's] saying:
4544 -. . . . . . . . . . . . . مِنْ صالِبٍ إلى رَحِمٍ ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(… from loins [ṣālib] to womb …)

semin-durr:8-8.t:
His saying: {إِنَّهُ}: the pronoun refers to the Creator, who is indicated by his saying «خُلِقَ» (he was created), because it is known that there is no creator other than Him.
His saying: {على رَجْعِهِ}: there are two views on the hāʾ. First: it is the pronoun of man, i.e. [able] to resurrect him after his death. Second: it is the pronoun of the fluid, i.e. He returns the semen into the urethra or the loins.

semin-durr:9-9.t:
His saying: {يَوْمَ تبلى}: there are several views on it. Abū al-Baqāʾ arranged them according to the disagreement over the pronoun, saying, on the view that the pronoun refers to man: "There are several views on it. First: it is governed by «قادر»." — Except that Ibn ʿAṭiyya, after reporting several views from the grammarians, said: "All these groups fled from making «لَقادِرٌ» the governing word, lest it appear from that that the power is restricted to that day alone." Then he said: "But when one reflects on the meaning and what the eloquent speech of the Arabs requires, it is permissible for «لَقادر» to be the governing word, because if He is able to do that at this time, He is all the more able at other times." — "Second: the governing word is implied, by way of clarification, i.e. He returns him on the day when [secrets] are tested. Third: its implied form is 'remember', so it would be a mafʿūl bihi (direct object). On the view that it refers to the fluid, what governs it is 'remember'." End of quote, in summary.
Some allowed the governing word to be «ناصرٍ». This is invalid, because what comes after the negative «ما» and what comes after the fāʾ cannot govern what precedes them. It has also been said: what governs it is «رَجْعِه». This is invalid, because a foreign element, namely the khabar (predicate), separates the maṣdar (verbal noun) from what it governs; though some tolerate this in the case of an adverb (ẓarf).

semin-durr:11-11.t:
His saying: {ذَاتِ الرجع}: it has been said: it is a maṣdar (verbal noun) meaning the return of the sun and the moon to it. It has also been said: [al-rajʿ is] rain, as in [the poet's] saying describing a sword:
4545 - أبيضُ كالرَّجْعِ رَسوبٌ إذا ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(Gleaming white like rain-water, sinking deep when …)
just as it was called awb (return), as in [the poet's] saying:
4546 - رَبَّاءُ شَمَّاءُ لا يَأْوي لِقُلَّتِها ... إلاَّ السَّحابُ وإلاَّ الأَوْبُ والسَّبَلُ
(A lofty, towering [peak]: nothing finds shelter on its summit but the clouds, the returning rain and the downpour.)

semin-durr:13-13.t:
His saying: {إِنَّهُ}: the reply to the oath in his saying «والسَّماءِ». Al-hazl (jest) is the opposite of seriousness and of rolling up one's sleeves in a matter. Al-Kumayt said:
4547 -. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... يُجَدُّ بنافي كلِّ يومٍ ونَهْزِلُ
(… every day [fate] is in earnest with us, while we jest.)
The pronoun in «إنَّه» refers to the Quran. It has also been said: to the preceding speech that indicates the resurrection and the raising up.

semin-durr:17-17.t:
His saying: {أَمْهِلْهُمْ}: this is the reading of the majority; since the command was repeated for emphasis, He varied the two wordings. From Ibn ʿAbbās: «مَهِّلْهُمْ», like the first. Al-imhāl and al-tamhīl mean waiting. One says: amhaltuka kadhā, i.e. I waited for you to do it. Al-mahl is gentleness and deliberateness.
His saying: {رُوَيْداً}: a maṣdar (verbal noun) emphasising the meaning of the governing word; it is the diminutive of irwād, by way of truncation (tarkhīm). It has also been said: rather, it is the diminutive of «رُوْد», and he recited:
4548 - تكادُ لا تَثْلِمُ البَطْحاءُ وَطْأتَه ... كأنَّه ثَمِلٌ يَمْشي على رُوْدِ
(The sandy valley-bed scarcely shows the dent of his tread, as though he were a tipsy man walking gently.)
Know that ruwaydan is used as a maṣdar in place of uttering its verb, so it is sometimes annexed, as in his saying {فَضَرْبَ الرقاب} [Muḥammad: 4], and sometimes not annexed, as in: ruwaydan zaydan. [It is also used as a verbal noun (ism fiʿl), in which case it does not take tanwīn but is indeclinable (mabnī) on fatḥa, as in: ruwayda zaydan.] It occurs as a ḥāl (circumstantial), as in: sārū ruwaydan, i.e. going slowly; and as a naʿt (adjective) of an omitted maṣdar, as in «ساروا رُوَيْداً», i.e. a slow journey. These rules have a place more fitting for them.
